mainTopic: Limits on redemption: borrowing or paying in parts (including for a מקדיש), and redemption by relatives for walled-city houses and an עבד עברי
overview: The גמרא first settles two clashing ברייתות about borrowing money to redeem and redeeming in parts: one follows רבנן and the other follows רבי שמעון. It then defends the earlier lesson that a מקדיש also cannot borrow to redeem or redeem in parts. רב אחא בריה דרבא attacks the comparison to a walled-city house, and רב אחא סבא rebuilds it from what an ancestral field and a walled-city house share. מר זוטרא attacks that shared feature, and רבינא saves the proof with an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew. Next, רב ששת rules that relatives cannot redeem a walled-city house. He is challenged from 'בכל גאולה תתנו' and from the triple 'יגאלנו', and the גמרא answers by reading those sources as being about unwalled houses and fields. Finally, the גמרא asks whether relatives can redeem an עבד עברי sold to a Jew. According to רבי they cannot. According to רבנן a proof is tried, rejected, and then the rejection is challenged.

steps.title: Finishing the earlier answer: one source follows רבנן, the other follows רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the previous discussion by assigning the two conflicting ברייתות to two different opinions: רבנן and רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one follows רבנן, and that one follows רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer from the previous discussion. Two sources seemed to disagree, and the גמרא says they simply follow two different תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real contradiction, because each ברייתא matches a different opinion. The ברייתא that forbids borrowing to redeem and redeeming in parts follows רבנן. The one that allows it follows רבי שמעון.

keyTerms.meaning: This one (pointing at one of two sources)
The Rabbis, the majority opinion
A תנא who disagrees with רבנן here

phrases.english: This one follows the Rabbis, that one follows Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the contradiction raised just before this section
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning each source to a different תנא (תנאי היא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to give opposite rulings on the same question.
steps.terutzMaskana: They reflect a known disagreement between רבנן and רבי שמעון, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: Two sources disagree about redeeming a walled-city house
steps.stepSummary: One ברייתא says a seller may borrow money to redeem and may redeem in parts; another ברייתא says he may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ברייתא teaches: he may borrow and redeem, and he may redeem in halves. Another ברייתא teaches: he may not borrow and redeem, and he may not redeem in halves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets two ברייתות side by side that give opposite rulings. Here they are about a house sold in a walled city (בתי ערי חומה).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the seller must have his own money, all at once, to buy back the house. One source says borrowing and partial payment are fine. The other says neither is allowed. This is a direct clash that needs an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: One ברייתא teaches
Borrows money and uses it to redeem
Redeems in halves, paying part now and part later
And another ברייתא teaches

phrases.english: One ברייתא teaches: he may borrow and redeem,
and he may redeem in halves;
and another ברייתא teaches: he may not borrow and redeem,
nor redeem in halves.
phrases.notes: The word אין at the start covers this part too, so read it as 'and he may not redeem in halves.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי חֲדָא: לֹוֶה וְגוֹאֵל וְגוֹאֵל לַחֲצָאִין, וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the same type of contradiction, now about walled-city houses
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of the ברייתות about redeeming a house in a walled city
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two authoritative sources give opposite rulings on the same case.

steps.title: Same answer: רבנן versus רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the walled-city contradiction the same way: one ברייתא follows רבנן and the other follows רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one follows רבנן, and that one follows רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is no real problem. The two sources follow the same two opinions it used a moment ago.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The disagreement between רבנן and רבי שמעון about borrowing and partial redemption also applies to walled-city houses. So the two ברייתות reflect that known dispute and do not contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no real contradiction

steps.whatToRemember: For both kinds of sale discussed here, the question of borrowing to redeem or redeeming in parts depends on the dispute between רבנן and רבי שמעון.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one follows the Rabbis, that one follows Rabbi Shimon.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא רַבָּנַן, הָא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning each source to a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות seemed to contradict each other about walled-city houses.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each one follows a different side of the רבנן and רבי שמעון dispute.

steps.title: A memory aid for the questions coming next
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives three code words to help remember which rabbis ask the coming questions and to whom.
steps.simpleTranslation: (A memory aid: חרש, חבש, זמן.)
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. The גמרא is setting up the next part by giving three code words that hint at the pairs of rabbis who will speak next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word is built from letters of the speakers' names. חרש hints at רב אחא בריה דרבא and רב אשי, who speak right after this. The other two words point to later pairs of speakers.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid, a code to help remember the order
The three code words for the coming speakers

steps.confusionAlert: These words are not part of the הלכה. They are only memory hooks for the names of the speakers.

phrases.english: (A memory aid: Cheresh, Chavash, Zeman.)
phrases.notes: Each word hints at a pair of rabbis about to speak. For example, חרש hints at אחא, רבא and אשי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A transition marker introducing a new series of challenges
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. It is a memory aid for the order of the speakers.

steps.title: The comparison between a walled-city house and a dedicator can be refuted
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא tells רב אשי that the earlier comparison fails. A walled-city house seller has weak redemption rights, while a מקדיש can redeem forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רבא, said to רב אשי: This can be refuted. What is special about one who sells a house in a walled city is that his power is weakened, since he cannot redeem it forever. Can you say the same about one who dedicates property, whose power is strong, since he can redeem it forever?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בריה דרבא attacks a comparison made earlier. That comparison learned a law about a מקדיש from the law of a house sold in a walled city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seller of a walled-city house can only buy it back within one year, so his rights are weak. The restrictions on him (no borrowing to redeem, no redeeming in parts) might come from that weakness. A מקדיש can redeem his field at any time, so his situation is different, and those restrictions may not carry over to him.

keyTerms.meaning: There is room to refute; the comparison can be broken
Houses in walled cities
His power is weakened
One who dedicates property to the בית המקדש
His power is strong

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic rule of comparing cases: if the source case has a special feature the new case lacks, the law cannot simply be carried over.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi:
There is a way to refute it:
phrases.notes: He is going after the comparison made earlier, on 20b, between the house seller and the מקדיש.

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְמוֹכֵר בַּיִת בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה –
phrases.english: What about one who sells a house in a walled city?
His power is weakened, since he cannot redeem it forever.
phrases.notes: After one year he loses the chance to buy it back. See ויקרא 25:30.

phrases.english: Will you say the same about one who dedicates property,
whose power is strong, since he can redeem it forever?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: מָה לְמוֹכֵר בַּיִת בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the first challenge announced by the memory aid (חרש)
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier comparison that learned the law of a מקדיש from a seller of a walled-city house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source case has a unique weakness, a redemption window of only one year, that the target case does not share. So the law cannot be carried over.

steps.title: Rebuilding the proof from an ancestral field and a walled-city house
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא סבא answers that we can still learn the rule for a מקדיש. He uses a במה הצד: the seller of an ancestral field proves the rule, and the walled-city house covers that case's weakness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא סבא said to רב אשי: The proof can come back another way. Let it come from a common feature of two cases. The seller of an ancestral field proves it: he can redeem forever, yet he may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts. If you object that the field seller is weak because he cannot redeem right away, then the seller of a house in a walled city proves it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא סבא defends the comparison against step 5's challenge. He starts building a new proof out of two sources instead of one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that a walled-city house is weak, since it can only be redeemed for one year, while a מקדיש is strong. So רב אחא סבא brings an ancestral field, which can be redeemed forever and still has the restrictions. Someone could object that the field is weak in a different way, since it cannot be redeemed right away. The walled-city house answers that objection, because it can be redeemed immediately.

keyTerms.meaning: A proof built from what two sources have in common
An ancestral field, inherited family land
Will prove (this case shows the point)
Borrowing money in order to redeem
Redeeming in parts, bit by bit

steps.confusionAlert: The two sources are not brought because each one is a perfect match. Each source covers the weak spot of the other.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא סָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha Sava said to Rav Ashi:
Because one can say: let the argument come back around,
phrases.notes: He means the proof can still be made, just built a different way.

phrases.english: let it come through a common-feature proof:
the seller of an ancestral field will prove it,
since his power is strong to redeem forever
and yet he may not borrow and redeem, nor redeem in parts.
What about the seller of an ancestral field?
phrases.notes: This is the objection someone might raise: the field seller is special in a weak way.

phrases.english: His power is weakened, since he cannot redeem right away.

phrases.aramaic: מוֹכֵר בַּיִת בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה יוֹכִיחַ.
phrases.english: The seller of a house in a walled city will prove it.
phrases.notes: That house can be redeemed right away, and it still has the same two restrictions.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר נֶיהְדַּר דִּינָא, תֵּיתֵי בְּמָה הַצַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5's challenge by replacing the single comparison with a two-source proof.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rebuilds the proof as a במה הצד from two sources
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Step 5 thought the proof fails because a walled-city house is weak and a מקדיש is strong.
steps.terutzMaskana: Using an ancestral field together with a walled-city house removes that weakness.

steps.title: The common feature applies to a מקדיש
steps.stepSummary: The two cases are different, but both can be redeemed and both have the two restrictions. So the same is true of a מקדיש.
steps.simpleTranslation: The argument goes back and forth. This case is not like that case. What they share is that they can be redeemed, yet one may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts. So I will bring a מקדיש: it can be redeemed, and one may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא סבא finishes his proof. He takes what the two cases share and applies it to a מקדיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each source alone could be objected to, but the objections cancel each other out. What remains is the feature both cases share: they are redeemable, yet borrowing and partial redemption are not allowed. A מקדיש is also redeemable, so the same restrictions apply to him.

keyTerms.meaning: The argument has come back around
This case is not like that case
The shared feature of both cases
Someone who dedicates his field to the Temple

phrases.english: And the argument has come back around,
phrases.notes: Each case can be challenged, and the other case answers that challenge.

phrases.english: this case is not like that case,
the feature they share is that they can be redeemed,
and one may not borrow and redeem, nor redeem in parts,
so I too will bring a מקדיש, which can be redeemed,
and one may not borrow and redeem, nor redeem in parts.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזַר הַדִּין, לֹא רְאִי זֶה כִּרְאִי זֶה, הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-source proof begun in step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Based on what the two cases share, a מקדיש may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts.

steps.title: Both sources are weak in the second year
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא attacks the shared feature. Both the field and the house cannot be redeemed in the second year, but a מקדיש can.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא בריה דרב מרי said to רבינא: This can be refuted. The shared feature is special because both are weak and cannot be redeemed in the second year. Can you say the same about a מקדיש, who is strong and can redeem in the second year?
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא challenges רב אחא סבא's two-source proof. He finds a weakness that both sources have and a מקדיש does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A walled-city house can only be redeemed in the first year, and an ancestral field cannot be redeemed until two years have passed. So in the second year neither one can be redeemed. A מקדיש can redeem at any time, including the second year, so maybe his rules are looser.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a refutation
His power is weakened
The second year after the sale

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari said to Ravina:
There is a refutation:
What about the feature they share?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן הוֹרַע כֹּחָם לִיגָּאֵל בְּשָׁנָה שְׁנִיָּה,
phrases.english: Their power is weakened, since they cannot redeem in the second year,
phrases.notes: The house can be redeemed only in year one, and the field only after two years, so neither works in year two.

phrases.english: will you say the same about a מקדיש,
whose power is strong to redeem in the second year?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: מָה לְהַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the shared feature that step 7 relied on.
steps.kashyaTarget: The הצד השוה built from the ancestral field and the walled-city house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both sources share a weakness, since neither can be redeemed in the second year. A מקדיש lacks that weakness, so the proof may not apply to him.

steps.title: A Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew proves the point
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers with an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew. He can redeem in the second year, yet he may not borrow or redeem in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to him: Because one can say that a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew proves it. His power is strong to redeem in the second year, and still he may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers מר זוטרא's challenge. He brings a case that can be redeemed in the second year and still has both restrictions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר זוטרא suggested that being able to redeem in the second year might make the rules looser. The עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew shows that this is not so. He can redeem in the second year, but the restrictions still apply. So the restrictions also apply to a מקדיש.

keyTerms.meaning: A Jewish servant
Who was sold to a non-Jew
His power is strong

steps.whatToRemember: The rule for a מקדיש is defended in layers. First a walled-city house, then an ancestral field together with that house, and finally an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew. In every case, being able to redeem does not allow borrowing to redeem or redeeming in parts.

phrases.english: Ravina said to him:
Because one can say:
a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew will prove it,
since his power is strong to redeem in the second year
and yet he may not borrow and redeem, nor redeem in parts.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר: עֶבֶד עִבְרִי הַנִּמְכָּר לְנׇכְרִי יוֹכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8's challenge with a new source that lacks the second-year weakness.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a counterexample (יוכיח) that removes the claimed difference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being able to redeem in the second year might allow borrowing to redeem or redeeming in parts.
steps.terutzMaskana: An עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew can redeem in the second year and still has both restrictions, so a מקדיש does too.

steps.title: Can relatives redeem a walled-city house?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חיננא asks רב ששת whether a sold house in a walled city can be redeemed by relatives. He lays out both sides: a גזירה שוה from שדה אחוזה would say yes, but maybe the גזירה שוה only teaches 'no redeeming in halves.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר חיננא asked רב ששת: If someone sells a house in a walled city, can his relatives redeem it, or not? Maybe we learn 'its redemption' and 'its redemption' from an ancestral field. Just as a field cannot be redeemed in halves but can be redeemed by relatives, so too this house cannot be redeemed in halves and can be redeemed by relatives. Or maybe, where the word 'redemption' is written about the field, it is written about halves, and it is not written about relatives?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רב הונא בר חיננא asks whether the seller's relatives may redeem a walled-city house, and he explains why both answers make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know the walled-city house borrows the 'no redeeming in halves' rule from the field through the shared word 'גאולתו'. The question is whether that word link brings over every redemption rule, including redemption by relatives. Or does it only bring over the rule the word 'redemption' is actually attached to, which is redeeming in halves?

keyTerms.meaning: Houses inside walled cities; the seller can redeem them only within one year
Redeemed by relatives: a relative buys the property back for the family
'Its redemption': the shared word that links the house to the field
In halves: buying back only part of the property at a time
'Or perhaps': introduces the other side of a question

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree that the house cannot be redeemed in halves. The question is only about relatives redeeming it.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana asked Rav Sheshet:
One who sells a house among the houses of walled cities,

phrases.aramaic: נִגְאָל לִקְרוֹבִים אוֹ אֵין נִגְאָל לִקְרוֹבִים?
phrases.english: can it be redeemed by relatives, or can it not be redeemed by relatives?
Do we learn 'its redemption' and 'its redemption' from an ancestral field?
phrases.notes: The same word appears for the house (ויקרא 25:29) and for the field (ויקרא 25:26), so one case teaches the other.

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה אֵינָהּ נִגְאֶלֶת לַחֲצָאִין
phrases.english: Just as an ancestral field cannot be redeemed in halves
and can be redeemed by relatives,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַאי נָמֵי אֵין נִגְאָל לַחֲצָאִין
phrases.english: so too this house cannot be redeemed in halves
and can be redeemed by relatives.
Or perhaps:
when 'redemption' is written about the field,
it is written about redeeming in halves,
but it is not written about relatives?
phrases.notes: The second side says the word link carries over only the rule that the word 'redemption' is attached to.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new but related question about the walled-city house, which was discussed in the earlier steps.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the גזירה שוה of 'גאולתו' carry over redemption by relatives from שדה אחוזה to בתי ערי חומה, or only the rule against redeeming in halves?

steps.title: רב ששת: relatives cannot redeem it
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that a walled-city house cannot be redeemed by relatives.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It cannot be redeemed by relatives.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת gives his answer: relatives may not redeem a walled-city house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת takes the second side. The word link teaches only the rule tied to the word 'redemption', which is redeeming in halves. Redemption by relatives does not carry over.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not redeemed by relatives

phrases.english: He said to him: It cannot be redeemed by relatives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A house in a walled city cannot be redeemed by the seller's relatives.

steps.title: A ברייתא includes houses in redemption
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חיננא challenges רב ששת from a ברייתא. The word 'בכל' includes houses and an עבד עברי in redemption, and 'houses' seems to mean walled-city houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him: 'And in all your land you shall grant redemption.' This comes to include houses and a Hebrew slave. Isn't this talking about houses of walled cities?
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא is brought to challenge רב ששת. It says the verse includes 'houses' in redemption by relatives, which seems to include walled-city houses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from 'בכל' that houses can also be redeemed by relatives. If 'houses' means walled-city houses, then רב ששת's ruling is contradicted.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him from a source
To include: a word in the פסוק adds more cases
A Jewish servant
'Is it not...?': suggests a reading that creates the challenge

phrases.english: He challenged him: 'In all... you shall grant redemption'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:24

phrases.english: This comes to include houses and a Hebrew slave.
Isn't this talking about houses of walled cities?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב ששת's answer in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that a walled-city house cannot be redeemed by relatives.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא includes 'houses' in redemption by relatives. If this means walled-city houses, relatives can redeem them.

steps.title: It means houses in unwalled towns
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the 'houses' in the ברייתא are בתי חצרים, houses in unwalled towns.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about houses in unwalled settlements.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ששת. It says the ברייתא is talking about houses in unwalled towns, not walled cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By reading 'houses' as בתי חצרים, the ברייתא no longer says anything about walled-city houses. So רב ששת's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in unwalled villages; the Torah treats them like fields

phrases.english: No, it means houses in unwalled settlements.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: 'houses' means a different kind of house.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא's 'houses' means houses in unwalled towns (בתי חצרים).

steps.title: Unwalled houses already have their own verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a verse would be needed for בתי חצרים, since the Torah already says outright that they are treated like fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: About houses in unwalled settlements, it is written outright: 'They shall be counted like the field of the land'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. Unwalled houses already have a clear verse that makes them like fields, so why would 'בכל' be needed to include them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah already says בתי חצרים are like fields, they get all the field's redemption rules from that verse. So reading the ברייתא as talking about them seems to make 'בכל' unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Outright, stated clearly
It shall be counted (treated as)

phrases.english: Houses in unwalled settlements:
it is written about them outright:
'They shall be counted like the field of the land'!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:31

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ברייתא's 'houses' means בתי חצרים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A separate verse already makes בתי חצרים like fields, so 'בכל' would be extra if it only taught the same thing.

steps.title: The verse makes redemption a duty, following רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'בכל גאולה תתנו' teaches that redemption by relatives is an obligation, following רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse comes to make it an obligation, and this follows רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The verse 'בכל' is not just repeating that unwalled houses can be redeemed. It teaches that redeeming is a duty, according to רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse 'like the field' only tells us that unwalled houses can be redeemed. 'בכל גאולה תתנו' adds that relatives are obligated to redeem. So the verse is needed, and the ברייתא still has nothing to do with walled-city houses, so רב ששת's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: To make it a fixed obligation
According to the opinion of רבי אליעזר

steps.whatToRemember: רב ששת rules that relatives cannot redeem a walled-city house. The ברייתא that includes 'houses' is about unwalled houses, and it teaches that redemption by relatives is an obligation, following רבי אליעזר.

phrases.english: That verse comes to make it an obligation,
phrases.notes: 'That verse' is 'בכל גאולה תתנו'. It means relatives must redeem, not just that they may.

phrases.english: and this follows the view of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14, which keeps the answer of step 13 and רב ששת's ruling in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the verse a new job: it teaches that redemption is a duty, not only that it is allowed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'בכל' would add nothing new for unwalled houses.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בכל' teaches that redemption by relatives is obligatory, following רבי אליעזר.

steps.title: The source: רבי יהושע says redeeming is optional
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the ברייתא behind step 15. It opens with רבי יהושע, who learns from 'ואיש כי לא יהיה לו גואל' that a relative may choose not to redeem.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'And he shall redeem what his brother sold' is optional. You say optional, but maybe it is required? The verse says, 'And if a man has no redeemer.' Is there anyone in Israel with no relatives at all? Rather, it means a man who has relatives who do not want to buy the land back, because the choice is theirs. These are the words of רבי יהושע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the ברייתא it relied on in step 15, starting with the opinion that disagrees: רבי יהושע, who says redeeming is optional.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every Jew has some relative, so 'he has no redeemer' cannot mean he literally has none. רבי יהושע reads it as: he has relatives, but none of them wants to redeem. That only makes sense if a relative is allowed to say no, so redemption is a רשות.

keyTerms.meaning: As a ברייתא teaches
Optional; you may if you want to
An obligation; you must
The verse teaches (says)
A redeemer, the relative who buys the property back

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:
"And he shall redeem what his brother sold": this is optional.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:25

phrases.english: You say it is optional,
or maybe it is really an obligation?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״וְאִישׁ כִּי לֹא יִהְיֶה לּוֹ גֹּאֵל״ –
phrases.english: The verse says: "And if a man has no redeemer":
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:26

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי יֵשׁ אָדָם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵין לוֹ גּוֹאֲלִים?
phrases.english: Is there anyone in Israel who has no redeemers?
Rather, this is one who does have relatives
but the relative does not want to buy it back,
since the choice is in his hands.
These are the words of Rabbi Yehoshua.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the ברייתא that step 15 relied on when it said 'following רבי אליעזר'. This half gives the opposing view of רבי יהושע.
steps.raayaObject: That the reading of 'בכל גאולה תתנו' as an obligation is a real תנאי opinion (רבי אליעזר), as opposed to רבי יהושע's view.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording the dispute between רבי יהושע and רבי אליעזר.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר says redeeming is required
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר learns from 'בכל גאולה תתנו' that redeeming a relative's sold land is a חוֹבָה. This is the opinion step 15 followed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: 'And he shall redeem what his brother sold' is an obligation. You say obligation, but maybe it is only optional? The verse says, 'In all your land you shall grant redemption.' The verse made it an obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives רבי אליעזר's opinion: redemption by a relative is required. This is the source step 15 was pointing to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תתנו', 'you shall give', is a command, so רבי אליעזר reads it as making redemption required. This confirms step 15: under the בתי חצרים reading, 'גאולה תתנו' teaches obligation, following רבי אליעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse fixed it (as a rule)
You shall grant redemption

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
"And he shall redeem what his brother sold": this is an obligation.

phrases.aramaic: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר חוֹבָה אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא רְשׁוּת?
phrases.english: You say it is an obligation, or maybe it is only optional?
The verse says: "In all... you shall grant redemption":
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:24. The dots skip the middle words, 'all the land you hold.'

phrases.english: The verse made it an obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same ברייתא. It gives the opinion step 15 relied on.
steps.raayaObject: Step 15's claim that 'גאולה תתנו' teaches that redemption is an obligation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אליעזר in the ברייתא: 'הכתוב קבעו חובה'.

steps.title: What is the word 'בכל' for? Left unanswered
steps.stepSummary: רבנן (or רבינא) point out to רב אשי that if the verse is about בתי חצרים, the extra word 'בכל' has no job. The question stays unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן said to רב אשי, and some say רבינא said to רב אשי: It works well for the one who says the verse comes to include walled-city houses. That is why 'in all' is written. But for the one who says it comes to include houses in unwalled towns, what is 'in all' for? It is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge to the answer of steps 13–15. Step 15 explained 'גאולה תתנו', but the word 'בכל' still has no job, and no answer is found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'בכל' sounds like it adds something new. If it adds בתי ערי חומה, that works well. But בתי חצרים are already counted as fields, and 'גאולה תתנו' was used for obligation, so 'בכל' adds nothing. The גמרא ends with 'קשיא': a real difficulty against רב ששת's side, even though it does not overturn his ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well (for one view), but...
According to the one who says
To include (an extra case)
Houses in walled cities
Houses in unwalled towns, which are treated like fields
It remains a difficulty, with no answer found

steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' here does not mean the הלכה is overturned. It means the question was never answered, so the reading 'houses means בתי חצרים' stays weak.

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rav Ashi,
and some say it was Ravina who said to Rav Ashi:
It works well for the one who says
that it comes to include houses of walled cities:
that is why "in all" is written.
But for the one who says
that it comes to include houses in unwalled towns,
phrases.notes: This is the answer from step 13, which defended רב ששת.

phrases.english: what is "in all" for?
It is a difficulty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 15 explained 'גאולה תתנו'. This step points out that the word 'בכל' is still left over.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 13 that the 'houses' included by 'בכל' are בתי חצרים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בתי חצרים are already counted as fields, and 'גאולה תתנו' teaches obligation. So 'בכל' adds nothing, which only works if it includes walled-city houses.

steps.title: אביי challenges from the triple 'יגאלנו'
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רב ששת from a ברייתא. The three times 'יגאלנו' appears include all redemptions in a set order, and that seems to include walled-city houses and an עבד עברי.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי challenged him: Why does the verse say 'he shall redeem him' three times? To include all redemptions, that they are redeemed in this order. Doesn't that mean walled-city houses and a Hebrew slave?
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge to רב ששת's ruling that walled-city houses cannot be redeemed by relatives. אביי brings a ברייתא that seems to include them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the repeated word 'יגאלנו' adds other kinds of redemption that follow the same order of relatives. אביי suggests these extra cases are בתי ערי חומה and an עבד עברי. If so, relatives can redeem walled-city houses, against רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him (from a תנאי source)
He shall redeem him
In this same order
Doesn't it mean...? (a suggested reading)
A Jewish servant

phrases.english: Abaye challenged him:
phrases.notes: He is challenging רב ששת's ruling from step 11.

phrases.english: Why does the verse say
"he shall redeem him," "he shall redeem him," "he shall redeem him," three times?
To include all redemptions,
that they are redeemed in this same order.
phrases.notes: The order of relatives in those פסוקים: first a brother, then an uncle, then other relatives.

phrases.english: Doesn't it mean houses of walled cities
and a Hebrew servant?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the 'בכל' challenge was left as a קשיא, a second ברייתא is brought against רב ששת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling (step 11) that relatives cannot redeem a walled-city house.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The triple 'יגאלנו' includes other redemptions done by relatives in order. The natural extra cases seem to be walled-city houses and an עבד עברי.

steps.title: The extra redemptions are unwalled houses and fields
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the redemptions added by the triple 'יגאלנו' are בתי חצרים and שדה אחוזה, not walled-city houses. So רב ששת's ruling stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means houses in unwalled towns and an inherited field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's reading. The extra redemptions are other things, so the ברייתא does not go against רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like step 13, the גמרא says the ברייתא is talking about property that relatives can already redeem: unwalled houses and inherited fields. Walled-city houses are not mentioned, so רב ששת's ruling survives this challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: An inherited family field
No (rejecting the suggested reading)

steps.whatToRemember: רב ששת's ruling, that relatives cannot redeem a walled-city house, survives both ברייתות by reading 'houses' as בתי חצרים. Still, the word 'בכל' was left as an unanswered קשיא.

phrases.english: No, it means houses in unwalled towns
and an inherited field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge by reading the included cases differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting which cases the ברייתא includes
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The triple 'יגאלנו' includes walled-city houses and an עבד עברי.
steps.terutzMaskana: It includes בתי חצרים and שדה אחוזה, so the ברייתא does not go against רב ששת.

steps.title: Houses in open areas and ancestral fields are already written explicitly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 20. בתי חצרים and שדה אחוזה are already stated outright in a פסוק, so why would the triple 'יגאלנו' be needed to add them?
steps.simpleTranslation: But houses in open areas and an ancestral field are written explicitly: 'They shall be counted with the field of the land'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. The two cases that the triple 'יגאלנו' was said to include are already written openly in the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 20 the גמרא said the three times 'יגאלנו' appears add בתי חצרים and שדה אחוזה. But a פסוק says houses in open areas are treated like fields, and fields can clearly be redeemed. So 'יגאלנו' seems to have nothing left to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in unwalled areas, which are treated like fields
An ancestral field, inherited land
It is written explicitly

phrases.english: Houses in open areas and an ancestral field
are written explicitly:
'They shall be counted with the field of the land'!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:31

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתֵּי חֲצֵרִים וּשְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה בְּהֶדְיָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of step 20
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the triple 'יגאלנו' comes to include בתי חצרים and שדה אחוזה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A derivation cannot be needed for something the פסוק already states openly.

steps.title: The closer relative redeems first
steps.stepSummary: 'יגאלנו' is still needed. It teaches the order of redemption: the closer relative comes first, as רב נחמן בר יצחק said.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב נחמן בר יצחק said: the closer relative comes first. Here too, the closer relative comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'יגאלנו' does not teach that these can be redeemed. It teaches who goes first: the closest relative.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fact that they can be redeemed comes from the explicit פסוק. The extra 'יגאלנו' adds a new detail, the order among relatives. רב נחמן בר יצחק said this rule elsewhere, and the same rule applies here.

keyTerms.meaning: Whoever is the closer relative comes first
So too, here as well

steps.whyThisMatters: The mention of רב נחמן בר יצחק leads the גמרא straight into the next topic, where his statement was first said.

phrases.english: As רב נחמן בר יצחק said:
the closer relative comes first,
so too here, the closer relative comes first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the derivation to teach a new detail
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'יגאלנו' is needed to show that these can be redeemed at all
steps.terutzMaskana: 'יגאלנו' teaches the order of redeemers: the closest relative goes first

steps.title: Where רב נחמן's rule was said: may relatives redeem a Hebrew slave sold to a Jew?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רב נחמן בר יצחק's rule was first said. It was said on a dilemma: may relatives redeem an עבד עברי sold to a Jew?
steps.simpleTranslation: Where was the statement of רב נחמן בר יצחק said? On this: they asked, may a Hebrew slave sold to a Jew be redeemed by his relatives, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to find the original setting of רב נחמן בר יצחק's statement. That setting is a new question about an עבד עברי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה clearly lets relatives redeem a Jew sold to a non-Jew. The question is whether the same applies when he is sold to a fellow Jew. This dilemma opens a new branch of the discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: Where was it stated?
A question was asked among them
A Jewish servant who was sold
Redeemed by relatives

phrases.aramaic: הֵיכָא אִיתְּמַר דְּרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק?
phrases.english: Where was the statement of רב נחמן בר יצחק said?
On this, for they asked:
A Hebrew slave sold to a Jew,
is he redeemed by relatives
or is he not redeemed by relatives?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכָא אִיתְּמַר דְּרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Traces the origin of the statement quoted in step 22
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether relatives may redeem an עבד עברי sold to a fellow Jew

steps.title: According to רבי there is no question
steps.stepSummary: According to רבי the dilemma does not start. He says that one not redeemed by 'these' relatives goes free after six years, which shows relatives do not redeem him.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי, don't ask. He says: one who is not redeemed by these is redeemed by six years. So clearly he is not redeemed by relatives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the question. According to רבי the answer is already known, so the dilemma only applies to another view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads 'באלה' (by these relatives) as pointing to a slave who goes out after six years. Going out after six years is the law of a slave sold to a Jew. So for רבי, such a slave is not redeemed by relatives.

keyTerms.meaning: According to רבי (יהודה הנשיא)
You should not ask the question
Evidently, this shows
He is not redeemed

phrases.english: According to רבי, you need not ask,
for he says: one who is not redeemed by these
phrases.notes: 'These' means the relatives listed in ויקרא 25:48–49. The word באלה itself comes from ויקרא 25:54.

phrases.english: is redeemed by six years,
so evidently he is not redeemed by them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the dilemma of step 23 by settling it for רבי
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רבי, a slave who goes free after six years (sold to a Jew) is not redeemed by relatives.

steps.title: The dilemma according to רבנן
steps.stepSummary: According to רבנן the question is real. Do we learn from the גזירה שוה 'שכיר-שכיר' that a slave sold to a Jew is like one sold to a non-Jew, or does 'יגאלנו' limit redemption by relatives to the slave sold to a non-Jew?
steps.simpleTranslation: Where you should ask is according to רבנן: what is the law? Do we learn 'hired worker' from 'hired worker' and not expound 'he shall redeem him'? Or perhaps 'he shall redeem him' means this one and not another?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets out the two sides of the dilemma according to רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the word 'שכיר' appears for both kinds of slave, so they share the rule of being redeemed by relatives. Side two: 'יגאלנו' (him) limits that rule to the slave sold to a non-Jew only.

keyTerms.meaning: Where you should ask the question
We learn a גזירה שוה from the word 'hired worker' appearing twice
For this one and not for another

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two slaves. The one sold to a non-Jew can clearly be redeemed by relatives. The question is only about the one sold to a Jew.

phrases.english: Where you should ask,
according to רבנן, what is the law?
Do we learn 'hired worker' from 'hired worker',
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:40 and 25:53. The word appears for both the slave sold to a Jew and the one sold to a non-Jew.

phrases.english: and not expound 'he shall redeem him',
or perhaps 'he shall redeem him'
means for this one and not for another?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ, אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבָּנַן מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates the dilemma of step 23 for רבנן, after step 24 settled it for רבי
steps.sheelahInformationSought: For רבנן, does the גזירה שוה carry over relative-redemption, or does 'יגאלנו' block it?

steps.title: Proof from 'In all ... you shall grant redemption'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says 'בכל' includes houses and an עבד עברי. The גמרא suggests this means walled-city houses and a slave sold to a Jew, which would answer the dilemma.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'In all ... you shall grant redemption' comes to include houses and a Hebrew slave. Doesn't this mean houses of walled cities and a Hebrew slave sold to a Jew?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to settle the dilemma with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'בכל' adds an עבד עברי to the cases that can be redeemed. If this means a slave sold to a Jew, then relatives can redeem him, and the question is answered.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, introducing a proof
Doesn't it mean ...?
Houses in walled cities

phrases.english: Come and hear:
'In all ... you shall grant redemption'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:24, the same פסוק רבי אליעזר used in step 17.

phrases.english: comes to include houses and a Hebrew slave.
Doesn't this mean houses of walled cities
and a Hebrew slave sold to a Jew?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the dilemma of step 25
steps.raayaObject: That relatives may redeem an עבד עברי sold to a Jew

steps.title: No, it means a slave sold to a non-Jew
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The ברייתא's עבד עברי can be one sold to a non-Jew, so the dilemma is not settled.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading the ברייתא another way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא means a slave sold to a non-Jew, it says nothing about a slave sold to a Jew, so the proof fails. The next step pushes back on this reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Sold to a non-Jew

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי, a slave sold to a Jew is not redeemed by relatives. According to רבנן it is a question. The proof from 'בכל' is turned aside here, but the next step pushes back on that answer.

phrases.english: No, it means a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 26
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The slave half of the proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's עבד עברי can be read as one sold to a non-Jew, so it does not prove anything about one sold to a Jew.

steps.title: The slave sold to a non-Jew is already written in the תורה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the דחיה. Redemption by relatives for an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew is written plainly in the פסוק 'או דדו או בן דדו יגאלנו', so the ברייתא's word 'בכל' cannot be needed for that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: But an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew already has it written outright about him: 'Either his uncle or his uncle's son shall redeem him'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is attacking the answer it just gave in Step 27. It says the case of a slave sold to a non-Jew does not need a hint from 'בכל', because the תורה says it openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא does not use an extra word like 'בכל' to teach something the פסוק already says clearly. So if 'בכל' adds an עבד עברי, it must be adding a new case, the slave sold to a Jew. That would bring back the proof from Step 26 and answer the question.

keyTerms.meaning: Clearly, openly, written outright
It is written about him
A non-Jew
His uncle
Shall redeem him

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new question. It pushes back against Step 27's answer, which reopens the proof from Step 26.

phrases.english: A Hebrew slave who was sold to a non-Jew,
it is written outright about him:
"Either his uncle or his uncle's son shall redeem him"!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:49. This פסוק is about the slave sold to a non-Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the דחיה of Step 27, which read the ברייתא's עבד עברי as one sold to a non-Jew.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 27 that the ברייתא's 'בכל' includes an עבד עברי sold to a non-Jew.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That case is already stated openly in the פסוק (ויקרא 25:49), so an extra word would not be needed to include it. The ברייתא must therefore mean a slave sold to a Jew.
